domains.title: Sosin, the Revealer of Things
domains.subtitle: messenger spirit who discloses hidden causes and conveys prayers
domains.lead: Sosin is the revealer or messenger spirit who discloses hidden causes, interprets omens, and carries petitions between humans and the spirit world in Korean tradition. The name means "Revealer of things" and belongs to the domain "Messenger, Revealer." Sosin is a spirit of revelation and communication in Korean shamanic cosmology, invoked to uncover hidden causes of illness, misfortune, or conflict. The name is interpreted as "revealer of things" or "messenger spirit," reflecting the figure's role in transmitting knowledge and petitions.

mythology.lead: The mythology of Sosin is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and by shamanic lineage.

myths.title: The Opener of the Way
myths.text: When a shaman begins a gut, Sosin is sometimes invoked to open the road between the human village and the spirit realm. Without this opening, prayers and offerings cannot reach their intended recipients.

myths.title: Revealing Hidden Causes
myths.text: If illness or misfortune has no obvious cause, the shaman petitions Sosin to reveal which spirit is offended, what taboo has been broken, or what offering is required.

myths.title: Carrier of Petitions
myths.text: Sosin carries the prayers and offerings of the living to higher celestial spirits and returns with their responses, serving as a postal and diplomatic figure in the spirit hierarchy.

etymology.derivation: The name is probably composed of 소 (so, "small" or an element in words of announcing/revealing) and 신 (sin, "spirit, deity"). Its meaning in shamanic usage emphasises disclosure and communication rather than hierarchy.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Sosin, the Hangul form is 소신. Hangul ‘소신’; no single canonical Hanja is fixed for this shamanic figure. The ASCII form sosin is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Sosin is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Sosin is primarily a shamanic figure and does not have a large presence in Confucian, Buddhist, or Daoist canonical literature. It belongs to the specialised pantheon addressed by mudang and reflects the Korean view that the spirit world is structured like a bureaucracy, with messengers, inspectors, and intermediaries. Scholars of Korean shamanism compare such figures to the spirit messengers found in other Central and East Asian religions, while practitioners treat them as necessary participants in ritual efficacy.
lore.culturalLegacy: Sosin is not a household name in the way that Yongwang or Samshin are, but it remains important within shamanic practice and the academic study of Korean religion. The figure appears in ritual manuals, recordings of gut performances, and ethnographic studies of mudang. It also interests people concerned with divination, intuition, and the hidden dimensions of experience. As Korean shamanism gains international scholarly attention, figures like Sosin help illustrate the complexity and sophistication of the tradition.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sosin invites reflection on the relationship between name, place, and identity. The restoration of the capitalised scholarly form is a small act of recognition: it marks the name as a proper noun of continuing significance in Korean culture and resists the flattening effect of ASCII-only domain names.
